questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the iliopubic tract?

options.A: It is a thickening of the lumbar fascia
options.B: It lies anterior to the Poupart’s ligament
options.C: It inserts into t he pubic tubercle in front of the conjoint tendon
options.D: Its fibers fan out with fascia iliaca laterally

explanation.text: The fibers of the iliopubic tract fan out with the fascia iliaca laterally. The fascia iliaca is a broad, fibrous sheet that covers the iliopsoas muscle and provides attachment for various muscles and structures in the hip and thigh region. Incorrect Options: Option A - It is a thickening of the lumbar fascia: This statement is incorrect. The iliopubic tract is not a thickening of the lumbar fascia.

It is a thickened band of fascia that runs parallel to the inguinal ligament. Option B - It lies anterior to the Poupart's ligament: This statement is incorrect. The iliopubic tract, situated deeper in the anatomical layers, runs parallel to the inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament) and lies posterior to it. Option C - It inserts into the pubic tubercle in front of the conjoint tendon: This statement is incorrect.
The iliopubic tract does not directly insert into the pubic tubercle. It blends with the transversalis fascia and forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

questions.question: Area marked in the given image supplied by dermatome number?

explanation.text: The area marked in the given image corresponds to the T10 dermatome. Each dermatome represents a specific segment of spinal nerve innervation. The T10 dermatome covers the region at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra, which is consistent with the location shown in the image.

Incorrect Options: Option A: T8: The T8 dermatome, positioned slightly higher on the trunk than the marked level in the image, provides sensory innervation to the skin at the eighth thoracic vertebra level. Option B: T9: The T9 dermatome, situated slightly above the marked level in the image, provides sensory innervation to the skin at the ninth thoracic vertebra level.
Option D: T11: The T11 dermatome, found slightly below the marked level in the image, provides sensory innervation to the skin at the level of the eleventh thoracic vertebra.

questions.question: Which of the following structures does not form the boundaries of the Calot triangle?

explanation.text: Gallbladder: The gallbladder is not considered one of the boundaries of the Calot triangle. The Calot triangle is an anatomical space located between the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and cystic artery. Incorrect Options: Option A: Common hepatic duct: The common hepatic duct is one of the boundaries of the Calot triangle. It carries bile from the liver and joins with the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

Option B: Cystic duct: The cystic duct is another boundary of the Calot triangle. It connects the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct and forms the neck of the gallbladder. Option C: Cystic artery: The cystic artery is also part of the Calot triangle. It arises from the right hepatic artery or its branches and supplies blood to the gallbladder.

questions.question: What is the vertebral level of the abdominal plane labelled 2?

explanation.text: The abdominal plane labeled as 2 is the Subcostal plane, also known as the "plane of the superior mesenteric artery." It's located just below the costal margin, connecting the 10th costal cartilages bilaterally. In the posterior aspect, it corresponds to the upper border of the third lumbar (L3) vertebra. This plane intersects with the aorta, inferior vena cava, and the third part of the duodenum.

Incorrect Options: Option A - lower border of L1 At the lower border of L1 is the location of the transpyloric plane, which is also known as the "plane of Addison." Option B - Upper border of L1 The upper border of L1 does not correspond to the subcostal plane. Option D - Lower border of L4 The lower border of L4 is the location of the intertubercular plane, which is also known as the "plane of the iliac crests.

questions.question: To what level of vertebrae does the given structure correspond?

options.A: At the junction of L1 & L2
options.B: At the junction of L2 & L3
options.C: At the junction of T12 & L1
options.D: At the junction of L3 & L4

explanation.text: The marked structure is the umbilicus which lies at the junction of L3 & L4. The umbilicus is located at the level of the intervertebral disc between the third lumbar vertebra (L3) and the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4). Associated structures at this level include the inferior vena cava, the renal veins, the gonadal arteries and veins, the ureters, and the descending colon.

Incorrect Options: Option A - At the junction of L1 & L2: Associated structures at this level include the spinal cord, the aorta, the inferior vena cava, the renal arteries and veins, and the ureters. Option B - At the junction of L2 & L3: Associated structures at this level include the inferior vena cava, the renal veins, the gonadal arteries and veins, and the ascending colon.
Option C - At the junction of T12 & L1: Associated structures at this level include the aorta, the inferior vena cava, the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery, and the renal arteries.

questions.question: A condition requires the surgery depicted in the image shown below. All the following are usually seen associated with this condition except?

explanation.text: Although renal anomalies can occur in Heterotaxy polysplenia syndrome, the absence of a kidney (unilateral renal agenesis) is not typically associated with this condition. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hepatic artery anomalies: Anomalies or variations in the hepatic artery can be seen in Heterotaxy polysplenia syndrome, as the condition affects the normal development and arrangement of abdominal organs.

Option C - Malrotation of the gut: Malrotation of the gut, where the intestines are not properly positioned during development, is a common finding in Heterotaxy polysplenia syndrome. Option D - Polysplenia: Polysplenia is commonly associated with the condition depicted in the image.

questions.question: What is the basis for the formation of omphaloceles?

options.B: Physiological hernia failing to go back

explanation.text: Omphalocele is believed to result from a physiological herniation of abdominal organs into the base of the umbilical cord during early fetal development. Normally, the abdominal contents herniate into the umbilical cord at around 6 weeks of gestation but then return back into the abdominal cavity.
However, in the case of omphalocele, this physiological herniation fails to go back, resulting in the persistence of the herniated organs outside the abdominal cavity.

Incorrect Options: Option A) Excessive length of the intestine: Omphalocele occurs due to a defect in abdominal muscle development, leading to organ herniation through the umbilical ring, not because of excessive intestinal length.. Option C) Herniation of liver: Omphalocele involves abdominal organs, like the liver, herniating through the umbilical ring. However, it's not only about liver herniation; other abdominal organs are also involved.
Option D) Herniation of umbilicus: Omphalocele does not involve the herniation of the umbilicus itself but rather the herniation of abdominal organs through the umbilical ring.

questions.question: At which vertebral level can the celiac vessel be observed in?

explanation.text: The celiac trunk emerges from the abdominal aorta just below the diaphragm's aortic opening, around the T12-L1 intervertebral disc level. It courses forward to the right and divides into three branches. Incorrect options: Option A. Coeliac vessel does not arise from T9 vertebral level. Option B. Coeliac vessel does not arise from T10 vertebral level. Option D. Coeliac vessel does not arise from L2 vertebral level.

questions.question: A 35-year-old female presents with persistent flank pain. An abdominal ultrasound reveals that the lower poles of both kidneys are fused. What is the most likely developmental cause of this condition?

options.A: Abnormal migration of the metanephros derivative
options.B: Failure of the ureteric bud to differentiate
options.D: Improper development of the urogenital sinus

explanation.text: This presentation is indicative of a horseshoe kidney. A condition where the lower poles of the kidney fuse during development. Normally, the Kidney ascends from the pelvis to its final position in the abdomen. Abnormal migration can prevent this ascent and lead to fusion. The ascent of the horseshoe kidney is blocked at the level of the inferior mesenteric artery. Development of the Renal System: Urogenital Sinus: (Option D) Forms the bladder.

Forms the urethra. Contributes to the lower 2/3rd of the vagina. Renal System Development Excretory Part Metanephrons Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubules, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubules. Collecting Part Ureteric bud Collecting duct, minor calyces, major calyces, ureter. Note: Metanephric Mesenchyme: Essential for kidney development.
The definitive kidney becomes functional by the 12th week of gestation, i.e., it begins excreting urine.
**Failure of the ureteric bud to differentiate (Option B):** would lead to malformations with the collecting system of the kidney and does not cause horseshoe kidney.
**Complete degeneration of the pronephros (Option C):** is a normal developmental process and does not cause a horseshoe kidney.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea is diagnosed with Mullerian agenesis. Which all structures are likely to be affected?

options.A: Fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper 1/3rd of the vagina
options.B: Uterus, epoophoron, and lower 2/3rd of the vagina
options.C: Fallopian tube, trigone of bladder, and clitoris

explanation.text: In females, the paramesonephric ducts, also known as Müllerian ducts give origin to the uterine tubes (fallopian tubes), the uterus, and the upper one-third of the vagina. Derivatives Wolffian Ducts (Mesonephric Ducts) Müllerian Ducts (Paramesonephric Ducts) In males Ureteric buds develop into ureters, pelvis, calyces, and collecting tubules of the kidneys.

Trigone of the urinary bladder Posterior wall of the part of the prostatic urethra Epididymis Ductus deferens Seminal vesicles Ejaculatory ducts Mesodermal part of the prostate Remains rudimentary and forms an appendix of testis In females Ureteric buds develop into ureters, pelvis, and calyces, and they collect tubules of the kidneys.
Trigone of the urinary bladder Posterior wall of the urethra Epoophoron Paroophoron - Gartner’s duct Uterine tubes Uterus Upper one-third of the vagina

questions.question: A 26-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department in active labour. The obstetrician is concerned about the size of the pelvic outlet and its implications for the delivery of the baby. Which of the following structures is NOT considered a boundary of the pelvic outlet?

options.A: Lower border of the pubic symphysis

explanation.text: Sacral promontory is a part of the pelvic inlet, not the outlet. Pelvis Components: Structures from anterior to posterior are: Urinary bladder Uterus (in females) Rectum Note: These components are supported by the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani and coccygeus).

Boundaries of the Perineum (same as pelvic outlet): Anteriorly: Lower border of the pubic symphysis (Option A) Arcuate or inferior pubic ligament Posteriorly: Tip of the coccyx (Option C) On each side from anterior to posterior: Conjoined ischiopubic rami Ischial tuberosity (Option B) Sacrotuberous ligament Openings in Perineum Males Females Urethra Anal canal Urethra Vagina Anal canal

questions.question: A 35 yr old male with injury to the perineum, presented with blood collection in the perineal area extending to the mid-thigh. Which of the following correctly describes the location and characteristics of the perineal space involved in this patient?

options.A: Obturator fascia and inferior pelvic diaphragm fascia meet to form its apex
options.B: Located below the perineal membrane, open anteriorly, and continuous with spaces in the scrotum and penis
options.C: It contains the urethral sphincter within the wall of the urethra
options.D: Wedge-shaped spaces located below the pelvic diaphragm on either side of the anal canal

explanation.text: Superficial perineal space is involved in this patient. Location: Superficial perineal space is situated below the perineal membrane, which separates it from the deep perineal space. Continuity: It is open anteriorly, allowing for continuity with other anatomical spaces. In males, this includes the spaces in the scrotum and penis, while in females, it connects to the clitoral region.

The Colles' fascia fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh, which typically prevents blood from spreading further into the thigh beyond this point. Perineal Regions: The perineum, located between the thighs, contains the external genitalia and is divided into two triangular regions: Anal and urogenital.

Region Description Anal Region Contains the anal canal and ischioanal fossa Urogenital Region Contains external urogenital organs Perineal Spaces: Space Description Superficial Perineal Space Located below the perineal membrane, open anteriorly, it connects with spaces in the scrotum/penis (males) or clitoris (females), enclosed posteriorly by Colles' fascia. (Option B) Deep Perineal Space Situated above the perineal membrane, previously thought to contain the urethral sphincter (now known to be within the urethra), it is thin and open above. (Option C) Ischioanal Fossa Wedge-shaped spaces in the anal triangle, located below the pelvic diaphragm, base formed by perineal skin, apex where obturator fascia and inferior pelvic diaphragm fascia meet. (Options A & D) Clinical Significance: 1.

Superficial Perineal Space Trauma: Straddle injuries may lead to hematoma or confined urine extravasation. Infections: Common site for Bartholin's abscess in females. Surgery: Involves structures like the penile/clitoral bulb for reconstruction. 2. Deep Perineal Space Urethral Injuries: Membranous urethra rupture can cause urine leakage, often in pelvic fractures. Surgery: Relevant in urethral repairs and sphincter interventions.

Incontinence: Damage to the external urethral sphincter may result in urinary issues. 3. Ischioanal Fossa Abscesses: Frequent site for ischioanal abscesses, which may cross the midline. Pudendal Nerve Block: Targeted here for regional anesthesia. Surgery: Key area for drainage of abscesses and treatment of anal fistulas.

questions.question: In a newborn presenting with ambiguous genitalia at birth, USG reveals the presence of a uterus. The karyotype was found to be XY. What is the most common cause?

explanation.text: Mutation in the SRY gene prevents the formation of testes Results in a lack of testosterone and Müllerian Inhibiting Substance (MIS). The absence of MIS leads to the proliferation of mullerian ducts (uterus present) and the lack of testosterone leads to degeneration of the wolfian duct. Genital System Development: Indifferent Stage: Both male and female structures can develop from common precursors.
Intermediate Mesoderm: A major portion of the genitourinary system develops from the intermediate mesoderm. Forms genitourinary ridges and ducts.

Genitourinary Ridges: Appears in 5th week of development Give rise to: Testis (in males): Appears in the 7th week of development Ovary (in females): Appears in the 8th week of development Kidneys (although the kidneys develop from the nephrogenic cord, which is part of the intermediate mesoderm, they are closely related to the genital structures during development).

Duct Types: Müllerian (Paramesonephric) Duct: Functional in females, develops into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and the upper 1/3rd of the vagina. Inhibited in males by Müllerian Inhibiting Substance (MIS) (also known as Anti-Müllerian Hormone or AMH), produced by Sertoli cells of the testes.

Wolffian (Mesonephric) Duct: Functional in males, it develops into epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts. (MNEMONIC- SEED: Seminal vesicle, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, ductus deferens) Regresses in females in the absence of testosterone. External Genital Development by Stage: Arises from the cloacal folds and genital tubercle (not the dorsal somatic lateral plate mesoderm).
Male and female external genitalia can be differentiated by 12-14 weeks of intrauterine life.

Structure Male Development Female Development Genital Tubercle Becomes the phallus (penis) Becomes the clitoris Urethral Folds Fuse to form the penile urethra Become the labia minora Genital Swellings Form the scrotum Form the labia majora Sex Differentiation: Male Development: SRY Gene: Located on the Y chromosome, it initiates the development of testes.

Activates downstream genes like SOX9 and SF1, which are essential for Sertoli and Leydig cell differentiation. Testosterone Effects: Testosterone, secreted by Leydig cells, stimulates the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts to form male reproductive structures (e.g., epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts). Dihydrotestosterone (DHT): Promotes the development of external genitalia (penis and scrotum).

Müllerian Inhibiting Substance (MIS): Known as Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) Secreted by Sertoli cells, it causes the regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, preventing the development of female reproductive structures. Female Development: Absence of SRY Gene: Without the SRY gene, the gonads develop into ovaries. Paramesonephric (Müllerian) Ducts: Develop into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper 1/3rd of the vagina.
External Genitalia: Develop in the absence of testosterone, forming the clitoris, labia minora, and labia majora.
**Excessive production of DHT (Option A):** promotes the development of male external genitalia.
**Inadequate expression of WNT4 (Option C):** No role in male development.
**Increased levels of estrogen (Option D):** Do not present with functional Müllerian ducts alongside regressed Wolffian ducts in a genetically male infant.

questions.question: A 16-year-old adolescent girl developed secondary sexual characteristics at 12 but has never menstruated. Ultrasound indicates no uterus. Karyotyping and hormone assays are normal. Which structure is most likely NOT affected in this patient?

explanation.text: The presentation is consistent with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome, characterised by Müllerian agenesis. In Mullerian agenesis, Ovaries are not affected. Ovaries develop from the genito-urinary ridge. Development of the Female Genitourinary System: Müllerian (Paramesonephric) Ducts: Origin: Mesodermal derivative.

Developmental Fate: Uterus Uterine (Fallopian) tubes (Options B) Cervix (Options D) Upper one-third of the vagina (Options C) Vaginal Development: Upper one-third: Derived from the fused Müllerian ducts. Lower two-thirds: Derived from the endoderm of the urogenital sinus. Urogenital Sinus: Origin: Endodermal derivative.

Forms: Urinary bladder Urethra Lower two-thirds of the vagina Mesonephros and Mesonephric Ducts: Mesonephros leaves two mesonephric ducts that open into the urogenital sinus. Mesonephric duct gives rise to the ureteric bud, which penetrates the metanephros, leading to the formation of the collecting system of the kidney. Wolffian (Mesonephric) Duct: Vestigial Remnants (in females): Epoophoron: Located above the ovary.
Paroophoron: Found near the ovary. Gartner’s duct: A remnant in the lateral pelvic area. Note: Remnants of the Mullerian duct (Paramesonephric duct) in males are the appendix of the testis.

questions.question: An 8-year-old male child presents with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Imaging studies reveal a significant dilation of the ureters and an abnormal configuration of the bladder trigone. The patient is diagnosed with vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Urologists suspect that the anomaly is linked to the embryological development of the trigone of the bladder. Which of the following statements about the trigone of the urinary bladder is FALSE?

options.A: The trigone is formed from the mesonephric duct.
options.B: The trigone is composed of endodermal tissue.
options.C: The proximal part of the mesonephric duct is the Wolffian duct. Mucosal rugosities are absent in trigone region.
options.D: The trigone is formed on the anterior wall of the bladder.

explanation.text: The trigone of the urinary bladder is derived from mesodermal tissue. Development of the Trigone of the Urinary Bladder: Origin: The trigone is formed from the absorption of the tip of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct into the posterior wall of the urogenital sinus. (Options A & D) Tissue Derivation: The trigone is composed of mesodermal tissue. (Option B) The remainder of the urinary bladder is derived from endoderm (urogenital

sinus). Mesonephric Duct: After the formation of the trigone, the proximal part of the mesonephric duct is referred to as the Wolffian duct. Unlike the rest of the bladder mucosa, which has rugae (folds) when empty, the trigone remains smooth regardless of bladder filling. (Option C) Clinical Significance: Anomalies in the development of the trigone can lead to urinary tract abnormalities.
Anatomical Significance: The trigone is an important landmark within the bladder, delineating the area between the ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.

questions.question: A one-day-old newborn is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to severe respiratory distress. Prenatal ultrasounds had revealed bilateral renal agenesis and severe oligohydramnios. The neonatologist explains that this malformation occurred early in gestation. Which of the following developmental processes is most likely responsible for the bilateral renal agenesis seen in this newborn?

options.A: Failure of the ureteric bud formation and induce the metanephric mesenchyme.
options.C: Failure of the mesonephric duct to fuse with the urogenital sinus
options.D: Failure of the mesonephric duct to differentiate into kidney

explanation.text: The ureteric bud is an outgrowth from the mesonephric duct and induces the metanephric mesenchyme to differentiate into nephrons (the functional units of the kidney). Hence, failure of the ureteric bud formation or not properly inducing the metanephric mesenchyme leads to bilateral renal agenesis. 1.

Collecting System (from Ureteric Bud): Forms: Ureter Renal pelvis Major calyces Minor calyces Collecting ducts (tubules) Potential Issues: If the ureteric bud splits too early, it may result in: Bifid ureter (two ureters) 2. Excretory System (from Metanephric Blastema): Each collecting tubule is surrounded by a metanephric tissue cap, which forms the excretory tubules.

Formation of Nephrons (functional units of the kidney): Proximal end: Forms Bowman's capsule, which surrounds a glomerulus. Distal end: Elongates to form the: Proximal convoluted tubule Loop of Henle Distal convoluted tubule Renal System Development Excretory Part Metanephrons Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubules, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubules. Collecting Part Ureteric bud Collecting duct, minor calyces, major calyces, ureter.

**Failure of the pronephros development (Option B):** The pronephros is the first, most primitive form of the kidney in early embryonic life, but it is non-functional in humans and regresses by the 4th week of gestation. Development or involution of pronephros has no significant role in the formation of the permanent kidneys.

**Failure of the mesonephric duct to fuse with the urogenital sinus (Option C):** A failure in this fusion would lead to malformations of the bladder or urethra, not bilateral renal agenesis. Ureteric bud and metanephric blastema interactions happen independently of this fusion process.

**Failure of the mesonephric duct to differentiate into kidney (Option D):** The mesonephric duct does not directly differentiate into the kidney. It gives rise to the ureteric bud, which then induces the metanephric mesenchyme to form the functional kidney.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches the embryonic structure with its corresponding differentiated structure in males and females during the development of external genitalia?

options.B: Genital fold → Labia majora (Female), Penoscrotal raphe (Male)
options.C: Genital swelling → Labia majora (Female), Glans penis (Male)

explanation.text: The urethral folds (often referred to as genital folds) develop into the labia minora in females and contribute to the ventral urethra in males. Development of External Genitalia: Structure Female Male Genital tubercle (phallus) Clitoris Glans penis Genital fold (urethral fold) Labia minora Penoscrotal raphe Part of the ventral urethra Genital swelling (labioscrotal swelling) Labia majora Scrotum

questions.question: During a pelvic exam, a gynaecologist is teaching the medical students about the structures of the vestibule of the vagina. Which of the following structures is NOT located within the vestibule?

explanation.text: The vestibule begins just below the clitoris and ends inferiorly at the posterior commissure of the labia minora. It contains the vaginal and external urethral orifices and the openings of the two greater vestibular glands (Bartholin glands) and numerous lesser vestibular glands. The clitoral glans is not located within the vestibule. Vestibule of Vagina: It is the area between the labia minora.

It is a smooth area that starts just below the clitoris at the top and extends downward to the posterior junction of the labia minora. Contents: External urethral orifice (Option A) Vaginal orifice (Option B) Openings of the two greater vestibular glands (Bartholin gland) (Option D) Openings of numerous lesser vestibular glands (Skene's Glands) - mucous-secreting glands.

questions.question: A 58-year-old male patient presents with difficulty in urination and reports a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. Upon examination, the neurologist suspects an issue with autonomic innervation to the urinary bladder. What are the root values for the sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation of the urinary bladder?

explanation.text: Urinary bladder is innervated by the vesical plexus, which comprises both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers, involving both motor and sensory functions. Sympathetic innervation controls bladder filling, whereas the parasympathetic innervation controls bladder emptying. Somatic innervation is responsible for the voluntary control of urination.

Type of Innervation Nerves Function Parasympathetic Nerve Fibers (S2, S3, S4) Pelvic splanchnic nerves Excitatory effect on Detrusor muscle Inhibitory to the vesical sphincter. Sympathetic Fibers (T10-L2) Inferior mesenteric plexus Hypogastric plexus Inhibitory effect on Detrusor muscle Motor action on vesical sphincter Somatic Nerve (S1, S2, S3) Pudendal nerve Supplies external urethral sphincter, which is under voluntary control

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with sharp pain and swelling in her right buttock and thigh after falling on her side, leading to difficulty sitting and walking. Examination shows swelling, tenderness, and bruising over the right buttock, with no deformity, dislocation, or neurological deficits, indicating a possible hematoma. What is the origin of the affected artery?

options.A: Anterior division of the internal iliac artery
options.B: Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
options.C: Anterior division of the obturator artery
options.D: Posterior division of the obturator artery

explanation.text: The scenario describes a hematoma resulting from trauma to the Superior gluteal artery, which is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. Superior Gluteal Artery Origin Branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.

Course Supply Superficial Branch: Gluteus maximus Deep Branch: Gluteus medius Gluteus minimus Obturator artery: Branch of the internal iliac artery Divides (at obturator foramen) into: Anterior (medial) and posterior (lateral) branches. Acetabular branch (posterior division) passes through the acetabular notch (supplying the fat in the acetabular fossa) and sends a twig to the head of the femur along the round ligament.
